figures.title: What survives the bottleneck
figures.caption: A phase table for a plain encoder–decoder. The encoder writes one annotation per source token; the bottleneck keeps only the final 256-float state, so five source tokens' 1,280 floats and fifty tokens' 12,800 floats must both fit in the same 256 slots. Bahdanau's addition keeps the annotations and lets every decoder step read them, but the recurrence remains.
figures.alt: A three-phase table with columns encode source, bottleneck, and decode target. The source-tokens row holds five or fifty tokens during encoding, is discarded at the bottleneck, and is empty during decoding. The annotations row holds one vector per source token, is discarded in plain seq2seq, and under Bahdanau is kept and read at every decoder step. The summary row holds the last encoder state, crosses the bottleneck as 256 floats, and becomes the decoder's start state. The target row is empty until decoding, where it holds one token per step.

data.note: Plain seq2seq keeps only h_T, so 1,280 or 12,800 floats of embeddings compress into 256 slots. The gradient back to the first source word is a product of T−1 Jacobians: with each factor 0.4, twenty steps give 0.4^19 ≈ 2.7 × 10^-8.

steps.label: The encoder reads the source one token at a time and writes an annotation per token.
Only the last state crosses the bottleneck; the annotations are discarded.
The decoder starts from h_T and emits one token per step.
Bahdanau keeps the annotations so each decoder step can score all of them.

figures.title: Additive scoring versus one dot-product matrix
figures.caption: At n = 20 decoder steps, m = 50 source positions, k = 128 and d = 512, additive scoring costs about 7.86M multiply-adds for the projections plus 128,000 for the per-pair dot, roughly 8M. Dot-product scoring costs 20 × 50 × 1024 = 1,024,000, about 16 times less. The penalty is the shape of the work: additive evaluates a tanh per pair, dot-product is one GEMM.
figures.alt: Two panels. Additive attention: e equals v transpose tanh of W1 h_j plus W2 s_i; the projections are GEMMs; the tanh runs over every one of the n times m pairs; at n equals 20, m equals 50, k equals 128 and d equals 512 the cost is about 7.86M plus 0.128M, roughly 8M multiply-adds, and it materialises a k by n by m intermediate. Dot product: e equals s_i transpose h_j; one GEMM S H transpose produces all n times m scores; 20 times 50 times 1024 equals 1,024,000 multiply-adds, about 16 times less arithmetic at these lengths.

figures.title: Softmax sharpens the weights; the alignment story is ours
figures.caption: Three annotations scored 2.0, 1.0 and 0.0 get softmax shares 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. Raising the first score to 4.0 gives 0.936, 0.047 and 0.017: the distribution sharpens toward a hard choice without becoming one. The weights are real numbers the model computed; reading them as word alignments is an interpretation, and Koehn and Knowles show it does not reliably hold.
figures.alt: Six horizontal bars in two groups. Before: h1 at score 2.0 has weight 0.665, h2 at score 1.0 has 0.245, h3 at score 0.0 has 0.090. After raising h1 to 4.0: h1 has 0.936, h2 has 0.047, h3 has 0.017.

data.note: e^2, e^1, e^0 = 7.389, 2.718, 1.000; sum 11.107. Raise h_1 to 4.0: 54.598, 2.718, 1.000; sum 58.316. The gradient through the softmax keeps a baseline, so the weights across source positions sum to zero in the score gradient. Koehn and Knowles (2017): attention weights are a poor guide to alignment.
